description: A deciduous shrub or small tree 1-4 m tall, growing as an upright clump of a few smooth grey stems. Each leaf is a feather of nine to thirteen toothed leaflets; flat-topped heads of small white flowers open in early summer, and by late summer they become heavy clusters of shiny orange-red berries about a centimetre across that hang on after the leaves have turned orange and fallen. In the Tetons it grows in the Douglas-fir forest and along the moist edges of the canyons, where bears and birds eat the berries in fall.

season_notes.winter: Bare grey stems, some still hung with shrivelled red berries above the snow.
season_notes.spring: Feathery leaves open late in spring.
season_notes.summer: Flat white flower heads in June and July, then green berries turning orange.
season_notes.fall: Orange-red berry clusters and orange to red leaves; black bears and robins strip the fruit.

notes: Rowan (the template) is the library's Sorbus, the same genus with the same pinnate leaves, white flower heads and red fruit clusters; it is a tree 3-7 m, so the card makes Greene's mountain-ash a multi-stemmed shrub or small tree 1-4 m (USDA PLANTS: growth habit shrub and tree, growth form multiple stem, erect, mature height 12 ft; Wikipedia: shrub or small tree up to 5 m). FEIS has no species review of Sorbus scopulina (its Sorbus sitchensis review, read, names it only as a species that hybridizes with Sitka mountain-ash; the guessed review URLs returned 404), so no FEIS value is used for it. Leaves pinnate, 9-13 leaflets (Wikipedia); leaf_size_m 0.15 for the whole leaf is the drafter's judgement; PLANTS: foliage green, fine texture, summer porosity moderate, fall conspicuous (hence a strong orange-red fall colour, its shade the drafter's). Flowers white to cream, five-petalled (Wikipedia; PLANTS: white, summer); the National Park Service's Grand Teton trees and shrubs page names the white clusters of mountain ash flowers in early summer, hence months 6-7. Fruit an orange to red pome about 1.5 cm (Wikipedia; PLANTS: red, summer to fall, persistent, abundant), so berries from August hanging on to January; the drawn cluster size is the drafter's. Habitat: the Douglas-fir placing on the Teton tile is from the brief; no allowed source read gives its habitat in detail, so the classes, shade 0.5 (PLANTS: shade tolerance medium) and the terrain weights are the drafter's judgement. PLANTS: resprouts, fire tolerance none. Elevation: no allowed source gave one; 1500-3000 m is the drafter's judgement for the Greater Yellowstone. Eaters: Wikipedia says birds and mammals including bears eat the fruit; the Grand Teton page says mountain ash berries appeal to bears, birds and other animals. The black bear and the American robin stand for them; no source read names a browser of this species (browsing by deer, elk and moose is reported by FEIS only for Sitka mountain-ash), so none is listed. cover_for is the drafter's judgement. Colours, crown profile, porosity, stems, bark, leaf-on months and densities are the drafter's judgement. A US Forest Service seed-manual chapter on Sorbus came up in a search but is not among the allowed sources and was not used.
